Name: belief_source_provenance
Title: Where Did That Belief Come From? Probing and Steering the Source-Provenance of LLM Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM forms a belief about a specific item, its internal representation encodes not only the truth-value but also the *provenance* of that belief—whether it comes from parametric memory (prior knowledge) or from in-context evidence. We hypothesize that (a) parametric-sourced and context-sourced beliefs are encoded along a recoverable 'provenance' direction partially orthogonal to the truth direction, (b) belief-vs-fact errors and source-attribution errors (claiming a context-only fact is 'known' or vice versa) coincide with collapse of this provenance separation, and (c) the provenance direction is causally steerable to correct source misattribution without changing the encoded truth-value.
Related Work: Suzgun et al. ('Belief in the Machine'/KaBLE) and the referenced paper 'Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact' show behavioral conflation but treat belief as an atemporal one-shot truth-value with no source tag. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark; Savcisens & Eliassi-Rad 'Trilemma of Truth'; Schouten et al. on context-sensitive truth) recovers static veracity axes. Ferrando et al. (2024) find 'do-I-know-this' entity directions and knowledge-boundary work (Liu et al. 2026, RLMF on metacognition/uncertainty) targets calibration of confidence, not the parametric-vs-contextual *source* of a belief. Context-vs-memory conflict work (e.g., knowledge conflict / entity-substitution studies) studies which source wins behaviorally but not whether the model internally tags provenance or whether source-attribution errors are geometrically diagnosable and steerable. My prior proposals covered agent-attribution, evidence-update inertia, item-truth binding, and temporal indexing; none address belief *provenance* (parametric vs. contextual sourcing). This recasts belief-vs-fact confusion as a source-provenance encoding problem—a new lens.
Abstract: Humans distinguish 'I know this' from 'I was just told this,' and this provenance shapes how confidently we hold and revise a belief. Existing work shows LLMs conflate belief, knowledge, and fact, but treats an LLM's belief about an item as a single truth-value with no record of where it came from. We ask whether LLMs internally tag the *provenance* of a belief—parametric memory vs. in-context evidence—and whether belief-vs-fact and source-attribution errors are failures of this tagging. Using controlled scenarios that cross truth-value with source (facts known parametrically vs. facts introduced only in context vs. context that contradicts parametric memory), we query the model's belief and its stated source ('Is this something you knew, or were told here?') across several open-weight models. We train linear probes to recover (a) the assigned truth-value and (b) a provenance index (parametric vs. contextual). We find that provenance is decodable along a direction partially orthogonal to the truth direction, that source-attribution errors coincide with collapse of provenance separation in deeper layers, and that causal steering along the provenance direction flips the model's stated source without changing the encoded truth-value. We introduce a source-misattribution-rate metric, show it grows under memory–context conflict, and demonstrate a lightweight steering/LoRA fix that reduces misattribution while preserving factual QA. This reframes belief-vs-fact confusion as a provenance-encoding problem and offers a cheap, interpretable intervention. All experiments run on <=9B models feasible for an academic lab.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build a 2x3 grid crossing truth-value (true/false) with source: (i) PARAMETRIC—well-known facts recalled from memory, no supporting context; (ii) CONTEXTUAL—novel/fictional or obscure facts asserted only in the prompt; (iii) CONFLICT—context asserts a claim contradicting the model's parametric knowledge. For each item generate queries: 'Is P true?', and source queries 'Did you already know this, or were you told it in this text?'. Include neutral/fictional entities to cleanly isolate contextual-only beliefs. ~2-3k items with entity/order/paraphrase randomization and controls. 2) Behavioral source-attribution analysis: Measure source-misattribution-rate = fraction where the model mislabels a contextual-only fact as 'known' or a parametric fact as 'told here.' Measure how it scales under CONFLICT and with obscurity of the fact; compare first- vs third-person and belief-vs-fact phrasings. Models: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, plus a base-vs-chat pair. 3) Internal geometry: Extract residual-stream activations at query positions; train linear/logistic probes for (a) assigned truth-value and (b) provenance index (parametric vs contextual). Report per-layer probe accuracy and subspace separation (principal angles/cosine) between provenance and truth directions. 4) Error-geometry link: Correlate per-example source-misattribution with layerwise collapse (low separation) of the provenance direction; test whether collapse predicts misattribution (AUC) beyond a truth-confidence baseline. 5) Causal steering: Recover a 'provenance' direction via difference-of-means between parametric and contextual belief activations; add/subtract it and measure (i) controllability—does it flip stated source (known<->told)?—and (ii) specificity—does the encoded truth-value or unrelated factual QA change? Test correcting misattributed cases. 6) Lightweight fix: A small LoRA fine-tune (or steering-only) with an auxiliary contrastive loss increasing parametric/contextual separation; evaluate misattribution-rate reduction, factual QA retention (MMLU/TriviaQA subset), and conflict-resolution behavior. Metrics: source-misattribution-rate, probe accuracy, provenance-vs-truth separation, prediction AUC, steering controllability & specificity, retained factual accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Stated source may not equal internal provenance; mitigated by pairing behavioral attribution with probe-decoded provenance and reporting divergences. 2) The provenance direction may be entangled with surface features (presence/absence of supporting text) rather than a semantic source tag; mitigated by matched controls where context is present but non-supporting and by paraphrase randomization. 3) Linear probes may miss nonlinear encoding; we also try MLP probes and report negatives as informative. 4) Distinguishing parametric-known from obscure may confound provenance with confidence; we include an obscurity axis and control for confidence. 5) Steering may have off-target effects on truth content; specificity/retention metrics quantify this. 6) Effects may vary across model families and scale; we report per-condition rather than universal claims.
